trees.title: Smoke from the car
trees.summary: You see smoke from the exhaust, from under the bonnet, from a wheel, or from inside the cabin.
trees.safety: Smoke from inside the cabin, a strong fuel smell, or smoke together with a burning smell of rubber or plastic — stop immediately, switch off the engine, and get out of the car with all the passengers.

n1.q: Where is the smoke coming from?

options.label: From around one of the wheels
From inside the cabin — the dashboard or under the seats

n2.q: What colour is the exhaust smoke?

options.label: White and thin, on a cold morning, disappearing after a minute or two
Thick white, continuing and sweetening the air

n5.q: What exactly do you see under the bonnet?

options.label: White vapour, not real smoke, together with rising engine temperature
Smoke with a burning smell of rubber or electrics
Smoke with a strong fuel smell

r-condensation-normal.text: Thin white vapour from the exhaust on a cold morning, which disappears after a minute or two of driving, is water condensed in the exhaust pipe — a completely ordinary occurrence in any car.

r-white-coolant-smoke.result: Suspected coolant burning in the combustion chambers
r-white-coolant-smoke.text: Thick white smoke that continues even after the engine has warmed up, and sweetens the air, points to coolant getting into the combustion chambers — usually a damaged cylinder head gasket.
actions: Stop in a safe place and switch off the engine.
Call for a tow; continuing to drive can destroy the engine.
For a further check: [[tree:engine-overheating|the engine is overheating]].

r-blue-oil-smoke.text: Bluish smoke, mainly noticeable on acceleration or after the engine has been standing for a while, points to oil getting into the combustion chambers — usually worn piston rings or valve seals.
actions: Check the oil level and top up if needed.
Go to a garage; the problem will only get worse over time, and will also increase oil consumption.

r-black-fuel-smoke.text: Thick black smoke points to a mixture that's too rich in fuel, usually because of a clogged air filter, a dirty fuel filter, or a sensor or injection fault.
actions: Go to a garage — this also hurts fuel economy and can damage the catalytic converter.
Don't ignore it even if the car still drives normally.

r-brake-smoke.result: A brake that has seized and overheated
r-brake-smoke.text: Smoke from around a particular wheel, unrelated to the exhaust pipe, points to a brake pad that has stayed pressed against the disc and is rubbing continuously — generating extreme heat that could ignite.
actions: Stop immediately in a safe place, without touching the hot wheel or disc.
Don't keep driving; call for a tow or roadside assistance.

r-electrical-smoke.result: A dangerous electrical fault — a fire risk
r-electrical-smoke.text: Smoke from inside the cabin, from the dashboard or from under the seats, with a burning smell of rubber or plastic, is always an emergency — a wire or electrical component overheating.
actions: Stop immediately, switch off the engine and the electrics, and get out of the car with all the passengers.
Move away from the car, and call Magen David Adom {{fact:emergency.mda}}, the police {{fact:emergency.police}} or the fire service {{fact:emergency.fire_and_rescue}} as needed.

r-fuel-smoke-danger.result: Suspected fuel leaking near hot parts — a fire risk
r-fuel-smoke-danger.text: Smoke under the bonnet together with a strong fuel smell points to fuel leaking and coming into contact with a hot part — a real and immediate fire risk.
actions: Stop immediately, switch off the engine, and get out of the car with all the passengers.
Move away and call the fire service: {{fact:emergency.fire_and_rescue}}.

r-steam-redirect.result: Probably vapour, not smoke — suspected overheating
r-steam-redirect.text: White vapour under the bonnet, together with rising temperature, is usually boiling coolant, not real smoke.
actions: Go to the dedicated tree: [[tree:engine-overheating|the engine is overheating]].
Don't open any caps while the engine is hot.
